title: SMCI Reports Tonight: Record Orders, Margin Recovery, and a Looming 10-K Deadline
subtitle: Super Micro Computer faces its moment of truth after the close — the cheapest AI infrastructure stock, with $60 billion in new orders and recovering margins, meets a skeptical market and a fiscal 2026 10-K due in 20 days.
summary: Super Micro Computer reports fiscal Q4 results after the close on August 11. Expected revenue of roughly $11.5 billion (about double year over year), gross margins guided to 15-17% after a July 21 pre-announcement, and a record $60 billion in new orders set up the print — while ~20% short interest, deeply negative free cash flow, and open legal and regulatory probes keep the stock priced for failure at ~10x forward earnings. Tonight shows whether the redemption arc is real.

bodyHtml:
Super Micro Computer reports fiscal fourth-quarter results after the close today, and it is hard to overstate what hangs on this print. The company enters the night as the cheapest name in AI infrastructure by a wide margin — shares trade near the low end of a 52-week range that tops out at roughly double current levels, at roughly ten times forward earnings and about half of sales. It is also the most contested: roughly one in five shares outstanding is sold short, and the options market is pricing in a move of around twelve percent in either direction. The stock has recovered from the depths of its accounting crisis, but the gains have been uneven — it is up only a couple of percent year to date while the AI infrastructure names it competes with have rallied anywhere from double to more than triple. Tonight is Super Micro's moment of truth: the final chapter of a redemption story, or another chapter of uncertainty.

The backstory matters, because it explains the discount. Two years of financial-reporting turmoil — restatements, delayed filings, and material weaknesses in internal controls flagged for a second consecutive year — turned the stock from darling to pariah. That history is why a company booking record AI server orders trades at a fraction of the multiples its competitors command. The overhang is more than reputational: a federal indictment of co-founder Wally Liaw over alleged Nvidia server smuggling to China, open SEC and DOJ probes, and an ongoing export-control review have kept the governance discount firmly in place. The investigations remain open, and none has produced a resolution — no fresh scandal, but no closure either. Tonight's numbers have to overcome all of it.

Start with margins, the metric that turned this quarter into a story in the first place. When Super Micro pre-announced on July 21, it guided gross margins to 15 to 17 percent — roughly double the 8 to 9 percent range it had flagged earlier in the year and a sharp recovery from the historic lows that followed its accounting troubles. If the final number lands in that range, it validates the operational turnaround; if it lands at the bottom, or management walks the guidance back, the bears win the night. Revenue is expected around $11.5 billion for the June quarter, roughly double the year-ago figure, and the company flagged more than $60 billion in new orders during the quarter — a single-quarter haul that exceeds Dell's entire $51 billion AI backlog. Watch whether that order flow converts into cash: free cash flow over the trailing twelve months is deeply negative, and at some point the balance sheet must catch up with the income statement. Analyst estimates for per-share earnings are scattered across an unusually wide range, a sign that even the professionals cannot agree on where the quarter landed. Guidance for the September quarter — and, more importantly, for fiscal 2027 — will tell investors whether the growth is durable or front-loaded.

The bull case is straightforward. Demand for AI servers is beyond dispute — Nvidia's Blackwell ramp is real, Dell's AI server revenue is up more than sevenfold year over year, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise just raised full-year guidance to 29 to 33 percent growth. Super Micro's direct liquid cooling technology gives it a genuine moat in the densest data center builds, and at ten times forward earnings and half of sales, the market is pricing in failure. The bear case is equally clear: financial controls that failed once can fail again, the cash burn is real, and the legal and regulatory cloud is not an event risk so much as a permanent discount. Short interest near twenty percent of the float means the stock is being actively bet against, not merely ignored. Both sides cite real numbers — that is what makes this name so polarizing. The bulls point to backlog, the bears to the balance sheet, and both are telling the truth.

Tonight's print is either the final chapter of Super Micro's redemption arc or another chapter of uncertainty, and the options market suggests investors expect fireworks either way. The orders are real, the margins appear to be recovering, and the stock is priced for the worst-case scenario. But the fiscal 2026 10-K is due August 31 — twenty days from tonight — and this is the third consecutive year of intense scrutiny around that filing. One clean report with results in the guided range, and the governance discount begins to close. Another miss, and the bears get their validation. Either way, tonight sets the tone for the second half of the year.
